## The Museum of Almost

The Museum of Almost is difficult to find, but not because it is hidden. It is difficult to find because it keeps moving.

Yesterday it was behind a laundromat. This morning it might be above a bakery, or in the quiet room of a closed library, or three doors down from a place that sells only blue ink. There is no permanent address. The museum prefers to appear somewhere people have almost forgotten to look.

Its collection is impossible to catalogue.

One room contains a left glove with no matching right. Another holds the name of a person you were about to remember but never did. There are dozens of letters written and never sent, keys found in places where their locks are no longer known, and songs that stop one verse before the part you loved most.

I went there once during a rainstorm.

The curator was an elderly woman named Mrs. Bell, who wore a red coat indoors and carried an umbrella full of other people’s umbrellas. She had opened the museum, she explained, because so many important things were being mistaken for nothing.

“Almost,” she said, “is not the same as never.”

She led me past a glass case containing a ticket stub for a concert that had been cancelled. Beside it rested a yellow umbrella that had kept its owner dry exactly once, on an evening when he no longer needed protecting from the rain. I did not understand the exhibit until Mrs. Bell told me that the man had carried it for twenty years because he liked remembering that evening.

In the next room were several almost-apologies.

They were beautifully preserved. One had been composed in the bus, rehearsed in the elevator, and abandoned at the front door. Another had been whispered into a telephone that disconnected halfway through the third word. A third had remained unsaid, though both people later agreed that it would have been easy to forgive.

I asked why the museum collected failures.

Mrs. Bell looked offended.

“These are not failures,” she said. “They are evidence.”

Evidence of what?

Of the lives that almost happened. The cities we nearly moved to. The conversations we nearly began. The selves we nearly became, before fear or habit or exhaustion persuaded us to remain who we were.

She opened a cabinet and removed a small glass jar. Inside was a curl of golden hair.

“My daughter’s,” she said. “From when she was very young. She cut it off before our trip to the sea, because she thought she would look silly in a photograph.”

Mrs. Bell placed the jar on a pedestal beneath a bright light.

“We never went,” she said. “She changed her mind about the sea, and then she changed her mind about the photograph, and then she grew up. But the hair was still part of the story.”

The rain had stopped by the time I left. The museum had closed, or perhaps it had simply become a bakery, which smelled faintly of cinnamon and regret.

On the corner, I found a small brass plaque half-covered by leaves. It read:

**Not everything needs to become something.**

**Some things are allowed to remain almost.**

I stood there for a while, holding a list of things I had almost said, in rooms where saying them might have changed everything.

Then I put the list in my pocket.

Not as a promise.

Not as a warning.

Just as proof that I had once come close.
